fixes.explanation: Easy one to slide into, friend, because it sounds so close. But the writer says faith is “…the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.” Nothing about what we can already see. The certainty is about what we do not see.

I get the thinking, since that's how my bakery works. You start with dough you can see. But the writer says what is seen “…was not made out of what was visible.” This universe was formed at God's command.

That's right, baker, and look at the order. The writer says “…before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God.” The commending comes first, then the taking up. If that were on my résumé, I'd frame it and hang it right over my ovens.

That one's out, friend. The verse says anyone who approaches God must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him. Seekers get rewarded, and the verse says nothing about God hiding.

Nice try, but that's not what Noah builds in this verse. The writer says that in godly fear, Noah “…built an ark to save his family.” A whole city is a lot of work, and I think an ark was plenty for one man's to-do list.

Yes, baker! The writer says Noah “…became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.” That happened by faith, right along with building the ark. By faith, the writer says, he also condemned the world.
That would be some inheritance, wouldn't it? I'd have to find a crown that fits over my chef's hat. But the verse says Noah “…became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.”

That's right, friend. The writer says that “…they saw them and welcomed them from afar.” That comes right after the writer says they died without having received the things they were promised. I picture someone waving hard at a bakery window from clear across the street.
Richer sounds nice, friend, and I'd take a fatter cookie box myself. But the verse says they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. That's the word for the blank.

I'm glad you checked, because it's actually the opposite. The writer says, “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.” They longed for a heavenly country, and God is not ashamed to be called their God. He has prepared a city for them.

Yes, friend! The writer says, “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.” That “Therefore” ties it back to their longing for a heavenly country. I think that's about the warmest line in the whole chapter.
